answer.text: Adds phosphate groups to tyrosines on its own cytoplasmic tails
answer.line: The insulin receptor is a receptor tyrosine kinase. Binding switches its kinase on, and it phosphorylates its own tyrosines.

steps: Name the receptor class first. Insulin uses a receptor tyrosine kinase, and the word kinase is the whole mechanism.
Insulin binds the outer part. The two halves then add phosphates to tyrosines on each other's tails inside the cell.
Those phosphotyrosines are docking sites. Relay proteins dock there and carry the message on, toward glucose uptake.

choices.text: Adds phosphate groups to tyrosines on its own cytoplasmic tails
choices.note: A kinase working on itself: autophosphorylation of its own tyrosines.

choices.text: Cleaves PIP2 into IP3 and DAG
choices.note: Splitting PIP2 is phospholipase C's job, downstream of a different receptor family. It is not the insulin receptor's first act.

choices.text: Carries insulin with it into the nucleus
choices.note: Riding the hormone to the nucleus is how steroid hormones work. Insulin is a peptide and signals from the surface.

choices.text: Opens as an ion channel and lets sodium in
choices.note: Receptors that open for ions, like the acetylcholine receptor at muscle, are a different class. Insulin's receptor is an enzyme.

choices.text: Exchanges GDP for GTP on an attached G protein at the inner surface
choices.note: Swapping GDP for GTP on a G protein is what a G protein-coupled receptor does, the other big surface class.

lockIt: Receptor tyrosine kinases phosphorylate their own tyrosines first; relay proteins dock on those phosphates.
